confirmed.statement: Study 1 states random assignment of individuals: 'Ninety-three participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups: exposed to ideas generated by a fine-tuned LLM (n = 46) or no exposure to LLM-generated ideas (n = 47).' The form's S1 quote is verbatim and its locator is right.
Study 1 repeats it in the procedure: 'The participants were randomly assigned to one group.'

Study 2 states random assignment: 'Participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups: use of LLM-generated ideas (n = 60) versus no use (n = 60).' The form's S2 quote is verbatim and its locator is right. 'Use' names the condition, not take-up: the AI arm had the ideas 'at their disposal' with 'no obligation to use them', so there is no self-selection into arms.
The abstract calls both studies 'randomized experimental studies'.
Both studies are one-way between-subjects designs with the individual as the unit, so unit = individual and structure = between are right, and no within-person order needs checking.

What was assigned is AI-generated material for the participant's own work. In Study 1 the AI arm saw, on the idea-submission page, '[Displayed list of 10 ideas randomly extracted from the database of AI-generated ideas]' and was told it could use them as inspiration but could not suggest an identical idea. Outcomes are scored on the participants' own ideas, so the arms do not differ only in whose output gets evaluated.
confirmed.locator: p. 14, Appendix B, Study 1, LLM-assisted human column; p. 7, Section 4.3, last paragraph; p. 8, Section 4.5, second paragraph

confirmed.statement: In Study 2 the AI arm saw four ideas 'randomly extracted from the database of AI-generated ideas' (different for each participant) under 'SUGGESTIONS GENERATED BY AN AI SYSTEM. Be free to ignore if not useful.' The database held 44 education-related ideas from the same generator.
confirmed.locator: p. 14, Appendix B, Study 2, LLM-assisted human column; p. 9, Sections 5.2 and 5.3

confirmed.statement: The tool is generative AI: 'Startup Ideas powered by OpenAI' (ideasai.net, accessed 15 July 2022), whose ideas were 'generated with GPT-3'. 488 LLM-generated ideas formed the database, and 453 remained after removing incoherent ideas and ideas that described an existing company. role = ideas_supplied fits codebook section 6.

confirmed.statement: The paper's 'fine-tuning' was done through prompting with past ideas labeled 'Good idea:' or 'Bad idea:' from online votes. The form hedges this correctly as a generator 'the paper calls fine-tuned'.
confirmed.locator: p. 7, Section 4.2; p. 13, Section 7, first limitation; p. 13, Appendix A

confirmed.statement: 'Static list of pre-generated ideas, no interaction with the model' follows the method sections: the ideas came from a fixed database and were shown as a list. The theory section's general claim that LLM stimuli are 'dynamically constructed at inference time rather than retrieved from a predefined repository' does not describe this experiment.

confirmed.statement: The comparison arms match the form (ai = none; ai_vs_bau). The Study 1 human-only column has the same scenario and instructions without the AI ideas, and both Study 1 columns say 'You can do some internet research if you wish', so web search is common to both arms and is not a separate aid. The Study 2 human-only column has the same EdTech scenario with no AI suggestions, and neither Study 2 column mentions internet research.

No other generative AI was available to either arm: Study 1 'was conducted before the release of ChatGPT so participants did not have another tool at their disposal', and in Study 2 'participants could not use other generative AI tools'.

The Study 1 human-only description's 'same ... Qualtrics interface' is supported ('The study used the same Qualtrics interface for both groups'), but on p. 7, not in Appendix B, which the description cites.

Arm counts match. Study 1 assigned 46 and 47 and analyzed 45 and 45 (90; three non-completers excluded). Study 2 assigned 60 and 60 and analyzed 59 and 58 (117; three participants excluded for unrelatedness). The per-arm drops (1 and 2 in each study) are the form's arithmetic, and the paper does not print them.
confirmed.locator: p. 6, Section 4.1; p. 8, Section 4.6; p. 9, Table 4; p. 9, Sections 5.1 and 5.5; p. 11, Table 6

confirmed.statement: preregistered = not_stated is right: the text mentions no preregistration, only an a priori G*Power analysis (f = 0.25, alpha 0.05, power 0.80, minimum 76 participants).

The paper draws its inference from AI versus no AI within each study: 'this conclusion is derived from comparisons between LLM-assisted and unassisted human conditions within each study'. The stimulus-pool comparisons (S1-O8, S2-O8) involve no assignment and are correctly kept as ai_vs_human context with question = none.
confirmed.locator: p. 11, Section 6.1, second paragraph; p. 13, Section 7, third limitation; p. 8, Section 4.6.2; p. 10, Section 5.5.2

summary: The PDF states random assignment in both studies (p. 6, Section 4.1; p. 8, Section 4.5; p. 9, Section 5.1): individuals in one-way between-subjects designs were assigned either to see a static list of GPT-3-generated startup ideas (10 in Study 1, 4 in Study 2) as optional inspiration for their own ideas or to work with no AI ideas, so criterion 1 holds. Every assignment, arms and ai_tool entry has explicit support, including the Ns, the internet-research line shared by both Study 1 arms (Appendix B, p. 14) and the statements that no other AI was available (pp. 6, 9), and the only gap is a locator: the Study 1 control arm's 'same Qualtrics interface' is on p. 7, not in Appendix B.
